chishang.intro: Chishang is a rice township in Taitung County, and the thing people travel here for is a farm road with one tree standing beside it. Mr. Brown Avenue runs through open paddy and is closed to cars, so the usual way to it is a bicycle rented outside the railway station. The bishop wood on it was planted by a farmer in the 1970s to tie his cattle to, and has been one of Taiwan's most photographed trees since an airline commercial was filmed under it in 2013.
chishang.meta_description: The Takeshi Kaneshiro Tree: a lone bishop wood in the rice paddies of Chishang, planted by a farmer in the 1970s and famous across Taiwan since 2013.
chishang.question_meta: The Takeshi Kaneshiro Tree is a bishop wood of roughly 50 years standing alone in a rice paddy on Mr. Brown Avenue in Chishang, Taitung County.
chishang.question_answer: The tree people come to Chishang for is the Takeshi Kaneshiro Tree, a bishop wood standing alone in a working rice paddy beside Mr. Brown Avenue, a farm road closed to cars about five kilometres from Chishang railway station. It was planted around the 1970s by the farmer Wu A-mu for shade and for tethering cattle, making it roughly 50 to 55 years old, and it took its nickname from a June 2013 EVA Air television commercial filmed under it with the actor Takeshi Kaneshiro.
chishang.question_context: Fame arrived fast and cost the tree something. Local tourism authorities put visitor spending at around NT$500 million a year at the peak, and the same period brought complaints about litter and about photographers walking into the crop, which is why the roots now sit inside a low fence. On 23 July 2014 Typhoon Matmo pushed the tree over; Japanese arborists Yamashita Tokuo and Kawaguchi Yoshihisa worked with Taiwanese colleagues to right it and treat it within days, and it was replanted on the same spot. It has recovered steadily and came through Typhoon Haikui in September 2023 with only minor branch damage. The sponsorship contract behind the nickname expired in 2023 and the official name reverted to the Fengcha Tree, the tea-offering tree, though almost nobody uses it. Mr. Brown Avenue itself is named after a different 2013 commercial, for a coffee brand, and is one of the best known cycling roads in eastern Taiwan.

faq.q: Why is it called the Takeshi Kaneshiro Tree?
faq.a: Because EVA Air filmed a television commercial under it in June 2013 with the actor Takeshi Kaneshiro. The nickname stuck. The airline's naming contract expired in 2023 and the official name is now the Fengcha Tree, the tea-offering tree.
Roughly 50 to 55 years. It was planted around the 1970s by the farmer Wu A-mu, who wanted shade and somewhere to tether his cattle.
Yes. It stands in a working rice paddy beside Mr. Brown Avenue, a public farm road. The roots are fenced to protect them, so you look at the tree from the path rather than walking up to the trunk.
Take a train to Chishang Railway Station, then rent a bicycle from one of the stalls outside it and ride about 5 km, roughly 30 minutes, along Mr. Brown Avenue. The avenue is closed to cars.

faq.q: Is it still standing after the typhoons?
faq.a: Yes. Typhoon Matmo toppled it on 23 July 2014 and a joint Japanese and Taiwanese arborist team righted and treated it within days. It has grown steadily since and came through Typhoon Haikui in September 2023 with minor branch damage.

trees.name: The Takeshi Kaneshiro Tree

location.address: Mr. Brown Avenue (Bolang Dadao), Chishang Township, Taitung County, Taiwan

trees.story:
A farmer planted this tree so he had somewhere to tie his cattle. Wu A-mu put it in around the 1970s, a single bishop wood in the middle of his rice paddy, good for shade and a tether and nothing else. In June 2013 EVA Air filmed a television commercial under it with the actor Takeshi Kaneshiro, and within a year the tree had a nickname, a fence around its roots, and an estimated NT$500 million a year in visitor spending attached to it. It also had photographers walking into the crop to get the shot.

Then on 23 July 2014 Typhoon Matmo pushed it over. Japanese arborists Yamashita Tokuo and Kawaguchi Yoshihisa came out with Taiwanese colleagues, righted it within days and treated it where it stood, and it was replanted on the same spot. It has grown steadily since and came through Typhoon Haikui in September 2023 with a few broken branches.

The sponsorship contract expired in 2023 and the official name reverted to the Fengcha Tree, the tea-offering tree. Nobody calls it that. It is about ten metres tall, barely a metre around the trunk, still alone in the paddy, and Mr. Brown Avenue past it is a farm road closed to cars. The usual approach is a rented bicycle from Chishang station and five kilometres of rice with no traffic on it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the only tree out there: one broad crown about ten metres high standing alone in the rice, with a low fence around its roots. It stands beside Mr. Brown Avenue, the farm road out of Chishang.
trees.access: Free. Stands in a working rice paddy beside Mr. Brown Avenue (Bolang Dadao), a farm road closed to cars but open to bikes and pedestrians; the tree is fenced to protect its roots but fully visible and photographable from the path.
trees.transport: Chishang Railway Station, then about 5 km (roughly 30 minutes) by rented bicycle along Mr. Brown Avenue; bike rental stalls sit right outside the station.

alishan.intro: Alishan is a mountain forest area in Chiayi County, reached by a narrow-gauge railway built to carry cypress down to the plains, and known for its sunrises, its sea of clouds and the giant red cypresses left standing in the recreation area. Its Sacred Tree is a title rather than a fixed tree. The original fell in the late 1990s, and the cypress carrying the name today was chosen by about 25,000 people in a public vote, on a 600 metre boardwalk near Ciyun Temple.
alishan.meta_description: The Sianglin Sacred Tree: Alishan's second-generation sacred cypress, chosen by public vote in 2006, 45 metres tall and 12.3 metres round.
alishan.question_meta: The Sianglin Sacred Tree is Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree, a red cypress 45 metres tall, dated at about 626 years by a 2022 study.
alishan.question_answer: The Sianglin Sacred Tree stands on Trail 1, a 600 metre boardwalk near Ciyun Temple inside the Alishan National Forest Recreation Area in Chiayi County. It is a Taiwan red cypress, 45 metres tall and 12.3 metres round by the park's own figures, and it was crowned Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree on 1 January 2007 after roughly 25,000 people voted for it the year before. Its age is disputed: tourism material has long said about 2,300 years, while a 2022 tree-ring study by National Chiayi University dated the main trunk at about 626.
alishan.question_context: The dispute has a straightforward explanation. The 2022 study, commissioned by the Forestry Bureau, found that the tree is a merged tree, several red cypress stems that grew into each other over centuries, so the standing mass is much larger than the age of any single dateable trunk would suggest. Neither figure is a mistake, and the older one is still the one most tourism material carries. Dimensions vary a little by source too: the park's own site gives 45 metres of height and 12.3 metres of girth, an older account 43.5 and 13.1, with a diameter at breast height of about 4.1 metres. The tree it succeeded, a red cypress of around 3,000 years, collapsed in heavy rain and was taken down in the late 1990s, which is why Alishan ran the vote at all. Before the crowning this one was known as the Guangwu Cypress, after a provincial governor's belief that it had germinated during the reign of the Han emperor Guangwu. The same boardwalk passes the Thousand-Year Cypress, the Tree of Three Generations and the Tree Spirit Pagoda.

faq.q: How old is the Sianglin Sacred Tree?
faq.a: Sources disagree and both figures are worth knowing. Tourism material has cited roughly 2,300 years for decades. A 2022 tree-ring study by National Chiayi University dated the main trunk at about 626 years, having found that the tree is several red cypress stems fused into one mass rather than a single trunk.

faq.q: Is this the original Alishan Sacred Tree?
faq.a: No. The original was a different and much older red cypress, which collapsed in heavy rain and was taken down in the late 1990s. The Forestry Bureau then ran a public online vote, about 25,000 people took part, and this tree was crowned Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree on 1 January 2007.
The park's own figures are 45 metres tall and 12.3 metres round, with a diameter at breast height of about 4.1 metres. An older account gives 43.5 metres and 13.1 metres.

No. Entry to the Alishan National Forest Recreation Area costs around NT$300, less for Taiwan residents and students, and the area is open year round. From the gate it is a short walk along the paved 600 metre Trail 1 boardwalk, past Ciyun Temple.
By the Alishan Forest Railway or the Alishan Route B bus from Chiayi Railway Station, roughly 2.5 to 3 hours. Both put you at Alishan Bus Station, just outside the park's entrance gate.

trees.name: The Sianglin Sacred Tree
trees.age_estimate: disputed: about 626 years by the newest study, versus a long-quoted 2,300 years

location.address: Trail 1 (the giant-tree boardwalk), beside Ciyun Temple and Xianglin Elementary School, Alishan National Forest Recreation Area, Alishan Township, Chiayi County, Taiwan

trees.story:
This tree was elected. Alishan's original Sacred Tree, a red cypress of around 3,000 years, was wrecked by storm damage and taken down in the late 1990s, and the Forestry Bureau put the succession to a public online vote. About 25,000 people took part, this cypress won, and on 1 January 2007 the county magistrate crowned it Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree. Before that it went by Guangwu Cypress, after a provincial governor's conviction that it had germinated during the reign of the Han emperor Guangwu.

Its age is genuinely in dispute, and both numbers are worth carrying. Tourism material has said roughly 2,300 years for decades, some of it stretching to 3,000. Then a 2022 tree-ring study by National Chiayi University, commissioned by the Forestry Bureau, dated the main trunk at about 626 years and explained the gap: what looks like one enormous stem is a merged tree, several red cypresses that grew into each other over centuries. The bulk is real. The single great age is not established, and the older figure is still the one most of the tourism material carries.

The park's own record gives it 45 metres of height and 12.3 metres of girth; an older account says 43.5 and 13.1. It stands on Trail 1, a 600 metre boardwalk near Ciyun Temple that passes the Thousand-Year Cypress and the Tree of Three Generations on the way, so it is a short walk in and not the only giant on it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 12.3 metres round and visibly several stems fused into one mass. It stands on Trail 1, the boardwalk running between Ciyun Temple and Xianglin Elementary School.
trees.access: Paid entry to Alishan National Forest Recreation Area (around NT$300, less for Taiwan residents/students), open year round; from the park entrance it is a short, easy walk along the paved 600 m Trail 1 boardwalk past Ciyun Temple.
trees.transport: Alishan Forest Railway or bus (Alishan Route B) from Chiayi Railway Station, roughly 2.5 to 3 hours; alight at Alishan Bus Station just outside the park's official entrance gate, then walk in.
